title: The Surface |X(z)|
intro: Most z-transforms met in practice are ratios of polynomials. Factored, the numerator gives the zeros and the denominator the poles, and those few points decide the shape of the whole surface.

blocks.text: The transforms of exponentials, sinusoids, finite pulses and every filter built from delays, adders and multipliers are rational: a ratio of two polynomials in $z$. Factoring each polynomial gives

blocks.tex: X(z) = g\, \frac{(z - q_1)(z - q_2)\cdots(z - q_M)}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2)\cdots(z - p_N)}

blocks.text: The $q_k$ are the zeros, where $X(z) = 0$, and the $p_k$ are the poles, where the denominator vanishes and $X(z)$ is infinite. Apart from the single constant $g$, the zeros and poles determine $X(z)$ completely. That is why a pole-zero plot, a few crosses and circles on the plane, is a full description of a filter up to its gain.
Taking magnitudes turns each factor into a distance:

$|z - q_k|$ is the distance from the point $z$ to the zero $q_k$. So the height of the surface at any point is the constant times the product of its distances to the zeros, divided by the product of its distances to the poles. Close to a pole one distance in the denominator goes to 0 and the surface shoots up; close to a zero one distance in the numerator goes to 0 and the surface drops to the floor.
In decibels the product becomes a sum, one term per zero and per pole:

Each zero contributes a funnel pointing down and each pole a funnel pointing up, all of the same shape, and the surface is just their sum. This is the view the viewer starts in. It is also why poles and zeros near each other nearly cancel: one funnel up and one down at almost the same place leave a small dimple.
The signal $x[n] = r^n \cos(\theta n) u[n]$ has

blocks.tex: X(z) = \frac{1 - r\cos\theta\, z^{-1}}{1 - 2r\cos\theta\, z^{-1} + r^2 z^{-2}} = \frac{z\,(z - r\cos\theta)}{(z - r e^{j\theta})(z - r e^{-j\theta})}, \qquad |z| > r

blocks.text: Two zeros sit on the real axis, at $0$ and at $r\cos\theta$, and two poles form a conjugate pair at radius $r$ and angles $\pm\theta$. Below with $r = 0.9$, $\theta = 60°$: two peaks above and below the real axis, a pit at the origin and a smaller one at $0.45$, and everything inside the circle $|z| = 0.9$ faded, because the sum only converges outside it.

items: Raise Tilt to 85° to look straight down: the coloured contours ring the poles and zeros of the z-plane panel.

Move Angle θ: the two peaks swing round the circle together, mirror images in the real axis. Real signals always have their complex poles and zeros in conjugate pairs, so the surface is symmetric about the real axis.
Move Radius r toward 1: the peaks climb toward the red ring and the response panel grows a sharp peak at $\omega = \theta$.

blocks.text: Poles and zeros at the origin and at infinity

A factor $z$ in the numerator is a zero at the origin; a factor $z$ in the denominator, as in $z^{-2} = 1/z^2$, is a pole there. Counting both, a rational function has as many poles as zeros if the points at infinity are included: $z/(z-a)$ has one zero at $0$ and one pole at $a$, while $1/(z-a)$ has one pole at $a$ and a zero at infinity (it falls to 0 as $|z|$ grows). The viewer draws only the finite ones.

Poles and zeros at the origin do not change the height on the unit circle at all, because every point of the unit circle is at distance 1 from the origin. They only add a delay or an advance, which shows up in the phase. The Unit Circle (#/math/z-transform/unit-circle) page uses this.

blocks.title: Read the height
solution: The distance from $-1$ to the zero at $1$ is $2$, and to the pole at $0.5$ is $1.5$. So $|X(-1)| = 2/1.5 = 4/3$.

blocks.title: Poles and zeros from a formula
blocks.text: Find the poles and zeros of $X(z) = \dfrac{1 - z^{-2}}{1 - 0.81 z^{-2}}$.
solution: Zeros at $\pm 1$, on the unit circle; poles at $\pm 0.9$, just inside it. On the unit circle the response is 0 at $\omega = 0$ and $\omega = 180°$ and close to 1.1 everywhere else: each pole sits right next to a zero and narrows its notch. It is a double notch that blocks the constant and the fastest alternation, not a band-pass filter.
